explanation: Fires on spatial/directional words that complete a 'facing/moving toward or from something' relation: prepositions or words after verbs of looking, pointing, flowing or emanating (staring to [the], out [of], pouring [from], looking [towards], [facing], in [front], [direction]). Also fires on 'is [subject] (to the license)' and 'available [from]'. Prepositions without a sense of direction or source fire weakly or not at all.

No shared pattern. Top examples mix URL slashes, markdown table pipes, code identifiers, quantifier words ('plenty', 'many', 'little', 'over'), punctuation in names and titles, and institution names. I can't predict new activations from these.

A mixture of unrelated triggers: subword pieces inside names or chemical words ('Do[ord]ash', 'di[ethyl]', 'do[led]'), the numerator right after '\frac{', and 'you'/'think' right after a question-initial 'Do' ('Do you think', 'Do you want'). The 'Do you' pattern gives moderate activation (20-50%).

Fires on focusing or restricting adverbs that add a qualifying clause after a statement, mainly 'especially' and 'particularly' after a comma or at sentence start, and also 'not even', 'at least' and 'not with'. The token after such an adverb ('especially [when]') gets weaker activation.

Fires in the opening 'Field of the Invention' sentence of patents, on the narrowing phrase 'and more particularly/specifically/in particular [to]'. The adverb or the following 'to'/comma fires strongly, as do the newline before 'The present invention relates'. Other patent boilerplate ('prior art', 'well-known', 'U.S. Pat.') fires weakly to moderately.

Strongest and most consistent on the '0' in '<?xml version="1.0"'. Also fires on assorted tokens in code, logs and technical text (Traceback, UserControl, dates in RSS headers, biomedical subwords), with no common thread among those.

Diffuse. It fires on version numbers after a product name ('Angular [1].x', 'iOS [6]', 'Explorer 1[0]'), on suffix pieces of adjectives (-ible, -uble, -ical), and on the second item in coordinated or contrasted lists ('wholesale and [retail]', 'or [large]', 'CVS'). I see no single concept.

Mostly fires in scientific or academic abstract and introduction text, on tokens that name a field or domain ('fields [in]', 'areas of [medical]', 'physics [and]', 'biological [and]'). It also fires on the first subword of rare proper names or medical terms ('[Tur]', '[epid]ural', '[Lov]ins'). The two sets look loosely tied by technical or academic register.

Mostly fires early in a document or title, on a verb, participle or function word right after the subject noun phrase ('Millions of Americans [stuck]', 'children [entering]', 'world [searches]', 'Whigs, Marxists, [and]'). Beyond being near the start of a sentence or title, I can't state a specific rule.

Fires on non-initial subword pieces of foreign or non-English proper names and words (Finnish, Portuguese, Spanish, Indian or Japanese place and person names, e.g. 'Noid[a]', 'Córd[oba]', 'Rhi[anna]'). Some English '-ly' suffixes also fire moderately.

Fires on the verb or preposition in a cross-reference to information found elsewhere: 'can be [found] [in] the LICENSE file', 'For details, [see]', '[listed] below/above', 'ask [in] the comments', 'reasons pointed [out]', 'alert us [via]'. It is strongest in license-header boilerplate.

Fires on middle or final subword pieces of rare proper names and technical words that are split into several tokens (Arabic, Turkish, Slavic or Latin names, drug and chemical names like 'isoproteren[ol]', hex strings). Ordinary English words do not fire.

Fires on the completing word of a common fixed phrase or compound, where the previous tokens make it predictable ('take a [look]', 'Escarp[ment]', 'Luteinizing [hormone]', 'Continuous [wave]', 'all that we [can]', '95% [CI]', 'do [it]'). Weak when the token is not a predictable completion.

Fires on programming and computing text about performance, profiling and compilation: words like 'performance', 'benchmarks', 'CPU', 'GHz', 'improve', compiler flags ('-O', '-m32', 'clang', 'pragma'), and some code or whitespace tokens in timing code. Code text that is not about speed or compiling fires weakly.

Fires on punctuation and separators at boundaries inside a list or citation ('Facility[;]', 'ALAIMO[*,]', commas and periods ending a clause, '([2])', '4[.]6 mm'), and on the first digit of a number. It looks like a general position or boundary detector, and I can't predict the strength from the token alone.

Fires on the second or later word of a multi-word proper name or compound noun, where the earlier words strongly predict it ('Queen [Mary]', 'fridge [freezer]', 'transmitted [disease]', 'San [Juan]', 'Medical [Research]', 'activity_horizontal[_margin]', 'num[_faces]'). Isolated words fire weakly.

Very mixed. It fires on items in lists of state codes and brands, on word endings in biomedical terms, on license boilerplate ('materials [provided]', 'GNU [Lesser]'), and on code paths and punctuation. I find no unifying feature.

Fires on approximators meaning 'nearly': 'almost' (strongest), 'nearly', 'virtually', 'just [about]', and Spanish 'casi'. It is strongest before quantifiers or absolutes ('almost none', 'almost always', 'nearly every').

Fires on evaluative or classifying adjectives that pick out a prominent subset in a noun phrase, mostly in scientific or formal text: 'important', 'major', 'critical', 'popular', 'well [known]', 'top', 'main', 'common', 'following', 'clinical'. It is strongest after 'of', 'most', 'the' or a number ('a number of [important] processes', 'four [major] types').

Fires on the token 'for' or 'For' when it is not an ordinary sentence-medial preposition: hyphenated compounds ('not-for-profit', 'taken-for-granted', 'All-for-Ireland'), code identifiers ('*ngFor', 'idForVideo', '--dump-forces'), and sentence-initial or quoted 'For'. Ordinary medial 'for' ('plan for', 'good for') fires moderately (30-50%).

Fires on list separators and the following list items, such as commas or semicolons between names or terms and items in quoted arrays ('Jul', [']Aug'). It also fires on assorted code and math tokens and subwords. Not specific enough to predict reliably.
